findings.title: Don't pipe an unpinned remote install script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` runs whatever that URL returns at build time, as root in the image. There is no version pin, checksum, or signature check. `-L` follows redirects to any host. Anyone who controls or compromises example.com, its CDN, or a redirect target can run any code in every image build, and the result ships with the image. Two builds of the same commit can also produce different images.

findings.title: Make a failed download fail the build instead of passing silently
findings.whyItBreaks: On Alpine, RUN uses /bin/sh, which has no pipefail, so the step's exit status is only sh's. If the network or DNS fails, curl writes nothing, `sh` gets empty input and exits 0, and the step succeeds. The image ships without whatever install.sh was meant to install. Without `-f`, an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page is also piped into sh and run as shell input. Either way, a failed download looks like a successful build.

findings.title: Don't pipe an unpinned remote script into sh during the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads whatever the remote host serves when the build runs, follows redirects with -L, and runs it as root inside the image. Nothing checks a checksum or signature and the script has no version pin. If the host or its DNS is compromised or the script changes, the published image is changed with no visible diff and builds can't be reproduced. The download can also fail silently. Without -f, curl exits 0 on HTTP 4xx/5xx and passes the error page to sh. -s hides curl's own errors. busybox sh in Alpine has no pipefail, so the exit status of the RUN line is sh's, not curl's. A network or HTTP failure can therefore produce an image that 'built successfully' but is missing whatever install.sh was supposed to install.

findings.title: Don't pipe an unverified remote install script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: Each build fetches https://example.com/install.sh with no version pin and no checksum or signature check, then runs it as root inside the image. Whoever controls that URL, its DNS or its CDN can change the script and put anything into every image built from now on. Builds can't be reproduced, because the script can change between builds. On top of that, `curl -sL` without `-f` plus a pipe means an HTTP error page, an empty response or a cut-off download still gets passed to `sh`. The step's exit status is sh's, not curl's, so a failed download can still produce a 'successful' image that is broken or only partly provisioned (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Stop LoadOrDefault conflating missing keys with stored empty values
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent (src/store.go:9-10) and (v, nil) when it is present. The new exported LoadOrDefault (src/store.go:15-18) drops the error with `v, _ :=`, so a missing key and a key explicitly set to "" both return "". The name says 'OrDefault', but there is no default argument and no way to tell a miss from a stored "". Callers that use this new API can therefore treat a missing key as a real empty value. Load is still exported, so this is a weak API contract rather than a defect with no workaround.

findings.title: Don't discard Load's error in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is missing (src/store.go:9-10) and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault drops the error with `v, _ :=`, so both cases return "". Any caller is forced to treat a missing key as a real empty value and may persist or act on it. The name also says 'OrDefault', but no default is accepted; the 'default' is just Go's empty string, which can also be a real stored value. Since this is a public function, the unusable contract is the defect even though nothing in the repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Wait for spawned sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent each result on the calling goroutine. When Run returned, all len(jobs) values had been delivered, in the same order as jobs. Now each send runs in a detached goroutine (lines 7-9) and Run returns at once. A caller that runs `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` (the standard producer pattern this signature invites) will race the close against pending sends and panic with 'send on closed channel'. A caller that reads len(jobs) values and assumes they line up with the jobs order now gets them in random order. If the receiver stops reading, the pending goroutines block forever and leak, because nothing waits for them or checks ctx. Run gives the caller no way to know when the sends are done.

findings.title: Wait for spawned senders before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every result before returning, so when Run returned all len(jobs) values had been delivered. Callers could safely do `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` or stop reading after Run returned. Now Run starts one goroutine per job and returns at once. (1) If the caller closes `results` after Run returns, a goroutine that has not sent yet panics with `send on closed channel` and crashes the process. (2) If the caller stops reading, every pending sender blocks forever. Nothing joins or cancels them, and `ctx` is still ignored, so goroutines leak. (3) Results now arrive in a scheduler-dependent order instead of job order, which breaks any consumer that matches outputs to inputs by position. Run is exported, so this new contract ships with the change even though no caller in this repo uses it yet.

findings.title: Wait for spawned sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `results <- j * 2` ran inside Run, so when Run returned every result had been delivered. Callers could safely do `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` or read exactly len(jobs) values and stop. Now Run starts one goroutine per job and returns right away, with nothing to wait on (no WaitGroup or errgroup). This causes three problems: (1) if the caller closes `results` after Run returns, a goroutine still sending on it panics with 'send on closed channel', which crashes the whole process; (2) if the caller stops reading, the goroutines stay blocked forever; (3) results now arrive in whatever order the goroutines run, not in job order. Run is exported, so a function that used to be synchronous now behaves asynchronously with no way for callers to know when it has finished. (ctx was already unused before this diff, so that part is not new.)

findings.title: Restore && so delete permission requires admin and the same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version allowed a delete only when the session was an admin AND the record was in the session's tenant. With `||`, two cases change. First, an admin of tenant A gets true for a record in tenant B (isAdmin=true makes the whole expression true), which breaks tenant isolation. Second, a non-admin user gets true for any record in their own tenant (tenantId match makes it true), so they can delete records they don't own and that only admins could delete before. canDeleteRecord is the exported delete-permission check, so every caller now allows these deletes.

findings.title: Restore admin AND same-tenant check in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, delete was allowed only when session.isAdmin was true AND session.tenantId matched record.tenantId. With ||, two new cases pass. (1) Any admin can delete records in another tenant: isAdmin=true with tenantId 'A' and a record in tenant 'B' gives true. That breaks tenant isolation. (2) Any non-admin user can delete any record in their own tenant: isAdmin=false with matching tenantId gives true. That breaks the admin requirement. canDeleteRecord is an exported authorization predicate, so any caller that gates deletes on it now allows both.

findings.title: Restore && in canDeleteRecord to keep admin and tenant checks
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, deleting required both an admin session and a matching tenant. With `||`, either condition alone is enough. So an admin from tenant A gets `true` for a record in tenant B (tenant isolation is gone), and a non-admin with session.tenantId === record.tenantId gets `true` (the admin requirement is gone). Both cases are authorization bypasses on a destructive action. canDeleteRecord is exported, so anything that relies on it gets the weaker check.

findings.title: Don't swallow parse errors; updateFontSize now saves defaults over bad data
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, malformed JSON or a bad theme/fontSize threw an error from parseSettings. That error reached updateFontSize (line 20) before save() ran on line 22, so nothing was written. Now the catch-all returns { ...DEFAULTS }. updateFontSize can't tell that apart from real settings, so it sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)). If the stored value is unparsable, it gets replaced with {theme:'light', fontSize:size}. For example, raw '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}' with a string fontSize resets the user's theme to light without any error. This loses data and permanently hides the corruption. parseSettings is exported, so every caller is also forced to treat a parse failure as if it were the real default settings.

findings.title: Don't map parse/validation failure to DEFAULTS; it overwrites saved settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch catches the JSON.parse SyntaxError and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' errors and returns { ...DEFAULTS } instead. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) calls parseSettings, sets fontSize and always calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)). Example: raw = '{"theme":"dark"}' (fontSize missing) or a truncated or corrupt file. Before this change the call threw and save was never called. Now it saves {theme:"light", fontSize:size}, permanently replacing the user's theme. The caller can't tell a failed parse from settings that really equal the defaults. parseSettings is exported, so every caller has the same problem: a failure looks like a real value.

findings.title: Stop parseSettings hiding parse errors; updateFontSize overwrites settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all at lines 14-16 turns every failure into `{ ...DEFAULTS }`: malformed JSON, `null`, a missing or wrongly typed theme, or a wrongly typed fontSize. Callers can no longer tell 'stored settings were invalid' apart from 'user chose light/14'. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) then saves that fallback. Example: raw = `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}`. Before, this threw 'bad fontSize' and save was never called. Now it saves `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}`, which silently overwrites the user's stored theme. The same happens with corrupt JSON: before, save was never reached; now the stored settings are replaced with defaults. parseSettings is exported, so external callers also lose the error signal.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the same commit that builtFrom reports
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is still `build.ref(branch)` (line 12), but `artifacts` now comes from `build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified"))`. If the branch head and the `verified` ref point at different commits, the report says it was built from commit X while listing commit Y's artifacts. The `branch` argument also no longer affects which artifacts are returned, so every branch gets the `verified` ref's artifacts. Callers relying on the exported `BuildReport` contract (artifacts belong to `builtFrom`) get wrong data.

After this diff it lists artifacts from `build.ref("verified")` (src/report.ts:13-14), which has nothing to do with the `branch` argument. When the branch tip differs from `verified`, the report says it was built from commit X but lists the artifacts of commit Y. The same `verified` artifacts come back for every branch, so callers of this exported function get artifacts that don't belong to the commit the report names.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit, not the 'verified' ref

The report says the artifacts were built from the branch commit, but they were actually built from the verified ref. That is wrong data on the public `buildReport` contract. findings.title: Restore the limit cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.' The new body returns [] when limit <= 0. With more than 20 inputs, `out[i] = page[i]` for i >= 20 grows the array, so renderFeed returns every entry instead of one page of 20. recentEntries is exported, so outside callers that size or paginate from `limit` also get uncapped results.

findings.title: Restore the `limit` cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 promises "at most `limit` entries". The old body did this with `.slice(0, limit)`. The new body returns the whole reversed array whenever limit > 0. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-12) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and allocates `new Array(20)`, but its loop runs to page.length. With 50 entries it writes out[20..49] and the array grows to 50, so the feed is no longer paged at 20. Every exported caller now gets more data than the contract allows.

findings.title: Restore the limit cap in recentEntries

findings.title: Restore execute() behavior instead of unconditionally throwing

findings.title: Viewer rejection in isEligible breaks handle()'s read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() first calls isEligible() and returns "rejected" if it fails (line 24). Only after that does it send viewers to "read-only" (line 25). With the new line 18, isEligible returns false for every viewer. Take a request with status="active", role="viewer", attempts=0. Before this change it got "read-only". Now line 18 returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24, and the line 25 branch can never run. isEligible is the gate for all of handle's outcomes, including the read-only one viewers are meant to get, so it should not reject them by role. Doing so blocks an outcome that was valid before.

findings.title: Keep viewer role out of isEligible so read-only access still works
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() calls isEligible at line 24 and then sends viewers to "read-only" at line 25. Before this change, {status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts:0} passed isEligible and got "read-only". With line 18 added, isEligible returns false for it, so handle returns "rejected" and line 25 can never run. The diff only changes isEligible and leaves handle's read-only viewer branch in place, which suggests the rejection was not intended.

findings.title: Don't let the payment gate block saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by two different actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `&& order.payment === "paid"` makes sense for submitting, but it now also runs for saving a draft. A draft order with no payment yet ({state:"draft", payment:"missing"}) gave `true` before this change and gives `false` now. saveDraft then returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving a draft shouldn't depend on payment, so users can no longer save drafts until they pay.

findings.title: Keep the payment requirement out of saveDraft's gate
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is the only gate for two different actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `&& order.payment === "paid"` makes both require payment. Saving a draft is fine on its own without payment, but now {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} makes saveDraft return "blocked" when it used to return "saved". Before this change, that order passed the gate ("draft" !== "ready" was true).

findings.title: Keep the payment requirement out of saveDraft's gate
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by two different actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Requiring payment makes sense for submitting, but saving a draft should not need it. Check with {state:"draft", payment:"missing"}: before this change canProceed returned true and saveDraft returned "saved". Now it returns false and saveDraft returns "blocked". findings.title: Take snapshot files from the channel head, not the stable head

For any channel other than "stable", including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main", the returned Snapshot claims to be commit X on channel C but lists the file tree of a different commit. publishSnapshot is exported, so external consumers that trust `commit` will publish or verify the wrong contents.

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int reject zero and negative values
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises the function only accepts positive integers, but the body is still plain `int(value)`. A negative amount becomes a credit, and a zero amount becomes a zero charge. Before the rename, `read_int` made no such promise. Now anyone reading the name will reasonably skip their own positivity check.

Anyone who sees a function called parse_positive_int will skip their own check.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy so apply_values doesn't mutate the caller's df
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values did `result = df.copy()` and wrote to the copy, so the caller's DataFrame stayed unchanged. Now `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` writes straight into the caller's DataFrame and returns that same object. Any caller that reuses the input afterward (to compare before and after, apply a second mapping to the original, retry, or hold a cached or shared frame) will silently see changed 'value' data. If 'value' is a new column, it also gets added to the caller's frame. The function name and its return-a-frame signature suggest it returns a new frame without changing the input, and that is no longer true.

findings.title: Restore df.copy() so apply_values doesn't change the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values copied the input (`result = df.copy()`), wrote the mapped values into the copy and returned it, so the caller's frame was never touched. Now `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` (src/transform.py:6) writes straight into the DataFrame the caller passed in, and the same object is returned (line 7). A caller that keeps using its original DataFrame, for example as a baseline, to compare before and after, or to retry, will silently see the overwritten 'value' column. Nothing signals this because a DataFrame is still returned. apply_values is a public module-level function, so changing it from 'returns a new frame' to 'modifies its input' changes what outside callers receive, even though no caller exists in the repo.

findings.whyItBreaks: The base version ran `result = df.copy()` and wrote only to the copy, so the caller's DataFrame was left alone. findings.title: Restore commit_id pin in fallback review POST
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview receives the headSha that was actually reviewed (runGithub @141, diff built from it @144). The main JSON POST pins commit_id: headSha (@89). The fallback runs whenever that POST throws (catch @100). The most common reason is a 422 from an inline comment whose line isn't in the diff. That fallback now sends only event and body. The GitHub Create Review API then attaches the review to the PR's current latest commit, not the reviewed one. If the author pushes while the review is running, the REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT verdict and its findings body (event from VERDICT_EVENT @48-52) land on a newer, unreviewed commit. Line references in the body point at the wrong code. The check-run is still posted against the old headSha (@128, @184), so the review and the check disagree on which commit the verdict covers. Before this PR, both POST paths pinned the reviewed SHA.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, normalizeFinding threw 'malformed finding: ...' for any of these: an invalid severity or category, a blank file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a lineStart/lineEnd that wasn't a positive finite number. Now each of those failures becomes a default that callers can't tell apart from real data. An unknown or missing severity becomes 'P1', which is a blocking severity, so junk output can request changes on a PR. An unknown category becomes 'bug'. A missing file becomes ''. A missing lineStart becomes 0, and a non-numeric one becomes NaN because nothing checks the result of Number(). Empty strings for whyItBreaks, suggestedFix and title are also accepted. The result is a 'valid' Finding with no location and an invented severity, and anything downstream will report or act on it as real. Also, a null or primitive entry in findings now fails with a generic TypeError on `raw.severity` instead of the specific malformed-finding error. normalizeFinding is exported, so this is the public contract whether or not anything in the repo calls it.

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview strict parameter and drop-invalid lenient mode
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `normalizeReview(raw, strict = true)` is now `normalizeReview(raw)`. TypeScript callers that pass a second argument stop compiling. Behavior changes in both modes. With strict=true (the default), a malformed finding used to fail the whole review; now it passes with made-up values. With strict=false, malformed findings used to be filtered out; now they're kept with defaults, and a null entry throws TypeError where it used to be dropped. Neither the strict nor the lenient behavior is available anymore.

findings.title: Stop turning malformed findings into default-valued findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw `malformed finding: ...` for: a non-object input; a severity outside P0-P3; an unknown category; an empty file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix; and a lineStart or lineEnd that is not finite or is <= 0. The head version only applies fallback values. Unknown severity becomes "P1" (line 98), so a garbage finding from the model now looks like a valid P1 finding. Unknown category becomes "bug". A missing file becomes "" (line 103). Missing line numbers become 0 (lines 104-105), and something like "abc" becomes NaN because there is no isFinite check. Missing title becomes "Untitled finding". Missing whyItBreaks or suggestedFix becomes "". The exported normalizeFinding, and normalizeReview through its map at line 131, now return these made-up findings where they used to throw. A caller cannot tell a model-output failure from a real finding, and it will report or gate on the made-up values. Also, normalizeFinding(null) now fails with a TypeError (`raw.severity` of null) instead of the explicit malformed-finding error.

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview's strict parameter and lenient-mode behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported, and its signature used to be (raw, strict = true). With strict=false it caught normalization errors and dropped the bad findings. The parameter is removed at line 113, and the try/catch filter branch is replaced by a plain map at line 131. TypeScript callers that pass `false` now fail to typecheck (too many arguments). JS callers have the argument silently ignored. Either way, lenient mode used to drop malformed findings and now keeps them with fallback values (P1, bug, file "", line 0), or throws a TypeError when an entry is null.

findings.title: Restore validation in normalizeFinding instead of defaulting bad fields
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to reject bad findings: wrong severity or category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a lineStart/lineEnd that is not a positive number. Each case threw an error. Now each failure is replaced with a default. An unknown severity (for example "high" or "critical") becomes "P1" at line 98, so the finding is reported as a P1 and can block a merge it shouldn't. An unknown category becomes "bug" (line 100-102). A missing file becomes "" (line 103). A missing lineStart becomes 0 (line 104), and a non-numeric one becomes NaN because Number("abc") is NaN and nothing checks it. Missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "" (lines 107-108). The result is a finding that cites no file or line, which the review contract forbids, and it still looks real. normalizeFinding is exported, so every caller now has to treat a malformed finding as a real one. normalizeReview also calls it at line 131, so malformed reviews are accepted instead of failing with a 'malformed finding' error.

findings.title: Keep the lenient mode that drops malformed findings in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported, and this diff removes its `strict` parameter. Before, calling it with strict=false skipped malformed findings, which a try/catch turned into null and then filtered out. Now normalizeReview(raw, false) still compiles in plain JS because the extra argument is ignored, but its behavior is different: findings are never dropped, and malformed ones come back as fabricated P1/bug entries. TypeScript callers passing the second argument will also fail to compile. In addition, a null entry in findings now crashes with a TypeError at `raw.severity` (line 96) instead of the old 'malformed finding: not an object' error. That breaks any caller that checks for the 'malformed' message.

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO" for gh pr view in the pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (lines 42-46). On a manual run, the working directory may not hold a checkout of this repo. The step env no longer has REPO and nothing sets GH_REPO, so `gh pr view` has to work out the repo from local git remotes, and it fails when there are none. The failure happens inside `$(...)` as an argument to `echo`, so the step still passes and writes empty `head=` and `base=`. `actions/checkout` (line 45) then gets `ref: ''` and checks out the default branch. The review step (lines 56-57) then gets empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA. The pull_request path is unaffected because it uses EVENT_HEAD. Severity is lowered to P2 because only manual runs are affected, and on this self-hosted runner a workspace left from an earlier run may hide the failure.

findings.title: Restore -R/GH_REPO so gh pr view can resolve the repo before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (line 42). Without `-R` or `GH_REPO`, `gh pr view` works out the repo from the git remote in the current directory. On a fresh or cleaned runner workspace there is no .git, so gh fails. The failure is hidden: the call is inside `$(...)` passed to `echo`, so the step's exit status comes from `echo` (0), and `head=` / `base=` are written as empty strings. actions/checkout (line 45) then gets `ref: ''` and checks out the default ref instead of the PR head. The review step (lines 56-57) gets an empty PR_BASE_SHA and the wrong PR_HEAD_SHA.

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO" on gh pr view; step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (lines 42-46). Nothing sets GH_REPO. Without `-R`, gh works out the repository from the git remote in the current directory. On a fresh or cleaned self-hosted workspace there is no git repo, so `gh pr view` fails. Because the call sits inside `$(...)` passed to `echo`, the step still exits 0 and writes `head=` and `base=` as empty values. With an empty `ref`, actions/checkout (line 45) falls back to the event ref, which for workflow_dispatch is the default branch. The review then runs on the wrong code with empty PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA (lines 56-57). The pull_request path (EVENT_HEAD set) is not affected.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output errors in normalizeReview instead of defaulting
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when the input was not an object or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks were missing or the wrong type. Lines 115-129 at HEAD turn every one of those failures into a default. summary becomes String(raw?.summary ?? ""), so a missing summary gives "" and a non-string one is coerced. findings, checked and residual_risks become []. So inputs like `null`, `{}`, a truncated or partial object, or `{findings: "oops"}` all return a RawReview with zero findings and zero blocking residual risks. That looks exactly like a real 'no defects' review. The Verdict type ('pass' | 'changes_requested' | 'needs_human' @src/shared/schema.ts:22) exists, but a caller can no longer route a reviewer failure to needs_human. normalizeReview is exported, so the public contract now merges the failure channel into the success channel for every external caller.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output rejection in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when the input was not an object, or when summary was not a string, or when findings/checked/residual_risks were not arrays. Now every one of those cases quietly falls back to a default: `raw?.findings` gives [], `raw?.residual_risks` gives [], `raw?.checked` gives [], and `String(raw?.summary ?? "")` gives "". So `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview("garbage")`, or `normalizeReview({summary:"x"})` all return {summary:'', findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That is exactly what a genuine zero-finding, non-blocking review looks like. A verdict built from RawReview (ReviewResult.verdict: pass|changes_requested|needs_human, schema.ts:75-83) can no longer tell a failed or truncated model reply from a clean review, so it would report a broken run as `pass` instead of `needs_human`. The function is exported and is the public parsing contract. Even with no in-repo caller, every future caller is forced to treat a parse failure as a clean review. Non-string summaries are also turned into strings (e.g. '[object Object]'), which hides a type error.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output errors in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when the input was not an object, `summary` was not a string, or `findings`, `checked` or `residual_risks` were not arrays. Now each check falls back to a default: `String(raw?.summary ?? "")` and `[]` for each array. So input like `null`, a non-JSON or truncated model reply, or `{findings: "oops"}` returns `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}`. That output is a valid RawReview with no findings and no blocking risks, which is exactly what a clean review looks like. A caller can no longer tell 'the reviewer output was broken' from 'the reviewer found nothing', so any verdict built from this result would report `pass` instead of `needs_human` or an error. The function is exported, so the broken contract is the defect even though nothing in the repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is still a trigger (lines 10-14), its required pr_number input is still passed to `--pr` (line 47), and the job `if` still lets dispatch runs through (line 24). But a dispatch event has no `github.event.pull_request`, so: (1) checkout `ref` (line 29) becomes `github.ref`, the branch the dispatch ran from (usually main), not the PR head. (2) BASE_REF (line 35) is hardcoded to 'main', which is wrong for PRs targeting any other branch. (3) PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) are empty strings. The removed step used to get these values from `gh pr view`. Now a manual review of PR #N runs on the wrong tree with empty SHAs. How badly that goes depends on how src/cli.ts handles empty SHAs, which can't be checked here, so this is P2 rather than P1.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has a required `pr_number` input and still passes `--pr <pr_number>` (line 47). A dispatch event has no `github.event.pull_request`, so: (1) line 29 resolves to `github.ref`, which is the branch the workflow was dispatched from (usually main), not the PR head. In this repo's self-review mode the checked-out src/ IS the tool (lines 3-5), so the wrong code runs against the wrong tree. (2) Line 35 falls back to 'main' even when the PR targets a different base branch. (3) Lines 45-46 set PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA to empty strings. Before this change, the removed `Resolve PR refs` step filled all three values from `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` on this path. Now the manual trigger, which exists to bypass the pull_request webhook, posts a review that does not match the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is still a supported trigger (lines 10-14: 'PR number to review (manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook)'), and the job gate at line 24 still lets it through. On that event `github.event.pull_request` is missing, so every changed expression either falls back or comes out empty. Line 29 `head.sha || github.ref` checks out the dispatch ref (usually the default branch), not the PR head. In this self-review repo the checkout's own src/cli.ts is the tool being run (lines 3-5), so the wrong code is installed and runs against the wrong tree. Line 35 `base.ref || 'main'` fetches main even when the PR targets another branch. Lines 45-46 set PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA to empty strings. The removed step used to fill them with `gh pr view $PR_NUM` (headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef). As a result, every manual review runs on the wrong commit, with no base/head SHAs and possibly the wrong base branch, which is exactly the case the dispatch trigger exists for.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer so git diffs over 1 MiB don't abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `maxBuffer`, spawnSync uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. If `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 100) writes more than 1 MiB, Node kills the child, sets res.error=ENOBUFS and leaves res.status=null. Line 12 (`status !== 0`) then throws, and runLocal fails before review() runs. The thrown message is also misleading: stderr is usually empty, so users see `git diff ... failed: ` and are never told about ENOBUFS, because res.error is not surfaced. Before this change the limit was 64 MiB, so a PR with a 1–64 MiB diff (lockfile churn, vendored or generated files) used to review fine and now always fails. The sibling `gh()` helper (line 36) still sets 64 MiB, so this was a deliberate limit.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync; diffs over 1 MiB now fail
findings.whyItBreaks: Without a `maxBuffer` option, spawnSync uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. If `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 100) prints more than 1 MiB, Node kills the child and sets `res.error` to ENOBUFS, with `status` = null. The `res.status !== 0` check at line 12 then throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty or unrelated stderr, so runLocal aborts before review() runs. PRs with lockfile changes, vendored files or generated code often pass 1 MiB, so local review stops working for them. They worked before this change (64 MiB limit). The sibling gh() helper at lines 33-37 still sets the 64 MiB limit, so dropping it here looks accidental.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync; large diffs now fail
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 bytes. The base version set 64 MiB. runLocal sends the whole patch through this helper (`git(['diff', baseSha, 'HEAD'])` @ src/adapters/local.ts:100). If a diff goes over 1 MiB, Node kills git with SIGTERM, sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null. `res.status !== 0` (line 12) then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with empty stderr, because res.error is never surfaced. Large PRs and lockfile-heavy diffs, which used to be reviewable up to 64 MiB, now cannot be reviewed at all, and the error message hides the cause. The sibling gh() helper (lines 33-37) still sets 64 MiB, so this looks like an accidental regression.

findings.title: Keep 'failure' conclusion when the review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: If the Needlefish check is required by branch protection, GitHub treats a completed 'neutral' conclusion like success. So any error during review (crash, timeout, bad model output, or gh failure in postReview) now lets the PR merge without being reviewed. The summary text even says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', but the conclusion now lets it through. Before this change, 'failure' blocked the merge.

findings.title: Take headSha from the reviewed checkout, not the live PR API
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha now comes from pr.head.sha, the PR head at the moment of the API call. The patch comes from `gh pr diff`, GitHub's current view. But changedFiles (line 144 → line 57 `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`) and repoPath (the code the reviewer reads) still come from the local checkout. If someone pushes after checkout, or on pull_request events where HEAD is the refs/pull/N/merge commit, these disagree. In the push race, postReview (line 85 commit_id) and postCheck (line 124 head_sha) attach an APPROVE / 'success' check to a commit whose code was never inspected. Changed-file classification and inline-comment filtering (line 63) can also disagree with the patch the reviewer saw.

findings.title: Large PRs now fail before the try block and post no check
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff` uses GitHub's diff API, which refuses large diffs (HTTP 406 'diff exceeded the maximum number of lines/files'). The local `git diff` it replaced had no such limit. ghText throws on that error (line 31), and line 143 runs before the try at line 179. So the error rejects runGithub without ever calling postCheck: large PRs that used to be reviewed now get no review and no check run at all.

findings.title: Restore "failure" conclusion for errored reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block runs whenever review() throws, or when postReview/postCheck throws (LLM error, timeout, gh failure, parse error). It now posts the Needlefish check-run with conclusion "neutral". GitHub branch protection counts a neutral check run as passing. If "Needlefish" is a required check, any review crash or provider outage turns into a mergeable PR. The summary text two lines below still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", which contradicts the conclusion. The error signal is turned into a value that branch protection reads as a pass, so it cannot tell "review failed" apart from "review allowed merge".

findings.title: Take headSha and patch from the reviewed checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha now comes from the live PR API (pr.head.sha) and the patch from `gh pr diff` (also the live PR head). changedFiles (line 144, changedFileSet uses `git diff baseSha HEAD` @57) and repoPath still describe the local checkout. In pull_request Actions runs, the local HEAD is the merge commit by default. It can also lag behind the PR if a commit is pushed after checkout. When they differ, the reviewer gets a patch that doesn't match the files it reads, and inline comments are filtered against the wrong path set. Worse, postReview (@85) attaches an APPROVE with commit_id = the newer pr.head.sha, so an approval and a success check get pinned to a commit whose tree was never inspected. Before this change, headSha and the patch both came from the local HEAD, so they were consistent.

findings.title: Keep the errored-review check-run as "failure", not "neutral"
findings.whyItBreaks: If the review throws (crash, model error, timeout), the catch block in runGithub posts the Needlefish check-run with conclusion "neutral" (line 191). GitHub branch protection treats "neutral" as passing for a required status check. So a PR whose review errored now shows a passing Needlefish gate and can be merged without any review. The summary on that same check still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", which contradicts the conclusion. Before this change the error showed up as "failure" and blocked merge. "neutral" is also what VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human maps to (line 53), so the gate can no longer tell a crashed review from a needs-human verdict. process.exitCode = 1 (line 196) only fails the workflow job's own check. It does not fix the Needlefish check-run, and that check-run is the one teams would mark as required.

findings.title: Restore trusted-main tool checkout; don't execute PR-head code as reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the tool came from frankekn/needlefish@main (trusted) and the PR was checked out separately into target/ as data only. Now there is a single checkout of `steps.refs.outputs.head` (line 46). `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) runs install-time scripts from the PR's package.json and lockfile. Then `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) runs the PR's own src/ with GH_TOKEN set, and the token has pull-requests:write and checks:write (lines 16-19). This causes three problems. (1) A PR can change src/ so that it always posts a passing review or check on itself, which defeats the review gate this workflow exists to enforce. (2) It runs untrusted code on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner (line 23), where install scripts and the CLI can persist on the host or read other secrets there. (3) On `workflow_dispatch`, the fork guard on line 24 is skipped (`github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || ...`), and line 39 resolves the head of ANY PR number, fork PRs included. So a maintainer who manually triggers a review of a fork PR runs the fork's code and install scripts with the write token on the self-hosted host. The old workflow avoided all three by never running PR-head code.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; PR head code now runs as its own reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the tool was checked out from frankekn/needlefish@main into ./needlefish and installed there, and only the PR head (./target) was untrusted. Now there is a single checkout of steps.refs.outputs.head (line 46). Line 51 runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the PR's package.json and lockfile, so the PR's lifecycle scripts and dependency sources run. Line 59 then runs the PR's own src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN (pull-requests: write, checks: write, lines 16-19) on a `runs-on: self-hosted` machine (line 23). Any PR author can change src/cli.ts to post a passing review or check for itself, which removes the review gate. The PR can also run arbitrary code on the persistent self-hosted host and use the write-scoped token. The fork guard on line 24 only covers the pull_request event. With workflow_dispatch, a maintainer can pass any PR number, including a fork PR, and line 39 resolves that PR's head SHA, which then gets checked out and run.

findings.title: Restore trusted-tool checkout; don't execute PR head code with secrets
findings.whyItBreaks: The tool checkout from frankekn/needlefish@main (the trusted copy) has been removed. Now `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) both run from the checkout of `steps.refs.outputs.head`, which is the PR under review. That means the PR's package.json lifecycle scripts, its lockfile-pinned dependencies and its src/cli.ts all execute on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner (line 23). They run under `zsh -l`, which loads the host's login profile and any API keys it sets, and with GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests:write and checks:write (lines 16-19, 56). Any PR can therefore (a) make its own review pass or post arbitrary review results, (b) steal the token and host credentials, and (c) leave persistent changes on the self-hosted machine. The fork guard on line 24 is skipped for workflow_dispatch: someone dispatching with a fork PR's number would run that fork's code. The new comment's claim that 'the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool' is the exact pattern the removed comment warned against: it 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.'

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization and conservative fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Before checking against SEVERITIES (line 85), the base code ran String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase(). The new code at lines 97-99 checks raw.severity exactly as given. So "p0", "P1 " or " p2" now fail SEVERITIES.includes(...) and hit the fallback, which also changed from "P1" to "P3". Example: a P0 finding written as "p0" was kept as P0 before and is now silently reported as P3. A missing or unknown severity now looks exactly like a real P3 instead of defaulting to P1. normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) maps every finding through this exported function, so every review result is affected.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and fail-closed default in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` used to accept model output like "p0", "P1 " or "p2" and map it to the right Severity. Now `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` is an exact, case-sensitive match. So raw.severity="p0" fails the check and becomes "P3", where before it became "P0". Missing or malformed severities also used to fall back to "P1" (treated as serious) and now fall back to "P3" (treated as minor). An exported normalizer therefore turns a critical finding with sloppy formatting into the lowest severity. Callers cannot tell that apart from a real P3, so any verdict or gating built on severity treats a P0 as a minor note.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and fail-safe default in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, raw.severity went through String(...).trim().toUpperCase(), so "p0", " P1 " and "p2" were accepted as P0, P1 and P2. Now raw.severity is checked against SEVERITIES exactly as given, so any case or whitespace difference fails the check. The fallback also moved from P1 to P3. Net effect: a model-reported "p0" (critical) becomes P3 (lowest), and a missing or garbled severity also becomes P3 instead of the safer P1. normalizeFinding is exported and is how normalizeReview (line 132) builds every finding, so this downgrade reaches every review result. The caller cannot tell a genuine P3 from a severity that failed to parse, so blocking findings can be reported as non-blocking.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, runCodex copied process.env, deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed the cleaned copy as `env`. The diff deletes that block and the `env` option, so spawnSync now inherits the parent's full process.env. The codex agent runs with cwd=opts.repoPath (the repo under review) and reads content an attacker can control: diffs, files, AGENTS.md. `-s read-only` limits filesystem writes but does not hide environment variables. Any GitHub credentials in the runner's environment are therefore available to the agent and to any tool it runs. A prompt injection in the reviewed repo could get the agent to print them into the review output that gets posted back.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing from codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, runCodex copied process.env, deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed that copy as `env` to spawnSync. The diff removes both the copy and the `env` option. Node's spawnSync falls back to process.env when no `env` is given, so the codex agent now inherits all three GitHub credentials. That agent reads repo content and PR prompts that may be attacker-controlled, which makes it a prompt-injection target. A token in its environment can be read through `env` or /proc and used with gh or the GitHub API. The `-s read-only` sandbox limits filesystem writes, not access to environment variables or the network, so it does not replace the scrubbing. Nothing else in the repo removes these variables (I searched with rg).

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, runCodex copied process.env, deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed the copy to spawnSync. Now the `env` option is gone, so Node passes the parent's full process.env to the codex child. That process reads untrusted PR diffs, repo files and prompts. Its `-s read-only` sandbox limits writes, not environment reads. So prompt-injected content can get the agent to read and echo credentials with write scope (for example from `env`). Those credentials can end up in the review output or logs. Nothing else in the repo strips these tokens (rg finds GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN nowhere else), so this removes the only protection.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running fork PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job runs on `pull_request` (line 8) on a `self-hosted` runner (line 18) and checks out the PR head SHA (line 23). It then runs `pnpm install` (line 28), which executes the PR's lifecycle scripts, and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) from the PR's own checkout. Both run under `zsh -l`, so they load the runner user's login environment. The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing keeping fork PRs off this runner. With it gone, anyone who opens a fork PR can run arbitrary code on the persistent machine. They can read the host user's dotfiles and credentials (for example model/API keys exported in the login shell), leave persistence behind for later trusted jobs, and reach the local network. GitHub's read-only fork token and withheld secrets do not protect the self-hosted host itself. Fork PRs also get a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, so the `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` posting in the review step would fail anyway. The guard removal exposes the host and gains no working fork reviews.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` and is triggered by `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened). It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (L23), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (L28) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (L34) from that checkout, all inside a login shell (`zsh -l`). The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing keeping fork PRs off this runner. Now any outside contributor can open a PR that changes src/cli.ts, package.json lifecycle scripts, or the lockfile, and that code runs on Frank's self-hosted machine. From there it can read whatever the host has (model API keys, ~/.config credentials, the login-shell environment), and it can persist on the runner to tamper with later jobs. GitHub's own guidance is not to use self-hosted runners with public-repo fork PRs for this reason. Fork PR tokens are read-only, so the `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` posting would fail anyway. Dropping the guard adds no working feature, only exposure.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow runs on `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) with `runs-on: self-hosted` (L18). It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (L23), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (L28), which runs dependency lifecycle scripts from the PR's package.json/lockfile. It then runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (L34), which is the PR's own source. Both steps use `zsh -l` login shells (L27, L31), so they load the runner host's profile and environment. The removed line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing stopping this job from running for fork PRs. Without it, anyone who can open a fork PR gets arbitrary code execution on a persistent self-hosted machine. They can read host credentials loaded by the login shell, plant persistent backdoors that affect later trusted runs, and tamper with later reviews. GitHub's fork-PR token restrictions do not help, because the attack is on the host, not on GITHUB_TOKEN.

findings.title: Accept explicit 0 for runner kill-delay env vars again
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs only feeds two settings: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (default 5000, L3-6) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (default 2000, L7-10). Both are used only as setTimeout delays (L123-124). Before this change, '0' was a valid value: 0 grace sends SIGKILL right after SIGTERM, and 0 give-up stops waiting right after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, Number('0') === 0 fails the check and falls through to fallbackMs. Anyone who set 0 to kill immediately now gets a 5 s SIGTERM grace and a 2 s give-up wait, with no error or log. The exported function's result for '0' also changes.

findings.title: Keep accepting 0 for runner kill-timer env overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the check was `parsed >= 0`, so `0` was accepted. With `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` you got SIGKILL right after SIGTERM, and with `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` the wait stopped right after SIGKILL. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` at lines 117-124 handles 0 fine. Now `0` fails `parsed > 0` at line 135 and silently becomes the fallback (lines 3-10): 5000ms grace and 2000ms give-up. Every timed-out run for these operators now waits up to about 7s longer, and nothing is logged. The function is exported, so its callers outside this repo also get `fallbackMs` instead of 0. The impact is extra latency, limited to the timeout path, so this is P3 rather than P2.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration now silently falls back to the default
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `readRunnerDurationMs("0", fb)` returned 0. With `parsed > 0` it now returns `fb`. With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, SIGKILL now comes 5000ms after SIGTERM (src/shared/runner-process.ts:124) instead of on the next tick. With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0, the give-up timer at src/shared/runner-process.ts:123 now waits 2000ms. Nothing warns about it, so an explicit operator setting is treated like invalid input, and a timed-out run can take up to ~7s longer than configured. `readRunnerDurationMs` is exported, so its public contract also changed: "0" now gives the same result as invalid input.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual_risks to the critic instead of []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, including `blocks:true` entries for unverifiable material gaps. The loop now reads only `res.findings` and `res.summary`, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hard-coded to `[]`. The critic never sees those blocking risks, so `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` at line 122 can return PASS even when a deep reviewer said a verdict could not be reached. That is a discarded failure signal: 'no risks' and 'risks dropped' now look the same.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files get deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: Hotspots now come only from `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6). The tail-coverage hotspot for uncovered `bundle.changedFiles` was removed. Some changed files never reach a deep pass: files the map model leaves out, and files that only appear in hotspots after the first six. Nothing records them in checked or residual_risks either, so the critic and the verdict assume the whole PR was reviewed.

findings.title: Keep a whyItBreaks component in the dedup key
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key is now `file|lineStart|category|title[0:60]` and no longer includes the whyItBreaks text. Two different defects at the same anchor line, in the same category, with generic titles now map to one key. Only the higher-severity one survives, so a real finding from another hotspot is silently dropped before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 93 keeps only the first MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 hotspots (`.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`; the constant is at line 26) and relies on the map model having assigned every file. The removed block collected every changed file not in the selected hotspots into a tail hotspot. Without it, files the map pass left out, and files that only appear in hotspots ranked 7th or later, never get a deep pass. Nothing records the skip (no checked entry, no residual risk), so a large PR can come back clean while some changed files were never reviewed.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual_risks instead of hardcoding an empty list
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, which can include blocks:true entries. Before this change they were collected into `residuals` and passed in candidateMerged. Now the loop drops `res.residual_risks`, and line 113 sends `residual_risks: []` to the critic. deriveVerdict at line 122 uses `pruned.residual_risks`, so a gap a deep pass marked as blocking never reaches the verdict. 'Cannot conclude' becomes indistinguishable from 'no risk', and the review can PASS when it should not.

findings.title: Keep whyItBreaks in the dedup key to avoid merging distinct findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key used to include the first 80 characters of whyItBreaks. Now it is only file|lineStart|category|title[0:60]. When deep passes overlap on the same file and report different bugs on the same line and category with similar generic titles, the findings get the same key and the lower-severity one is silently dropped before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so files outside top hotspots are reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: `hotspots` is now `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 @L26). Large mode runs when there are more than 10 changed files (L30). Any changed file the map pass leaves out of every hotspot, or that only appears in hotspots ranked 7th or lower, is never sent to a deep pass. Nothing records the gap: no tail hotspot and no residual risk. The critic only sees the merged findings and the patchStat, and deriveVerdict (L122) gets no signal that files were skipped, so a PR can PASS with unreviewed changed files. The removed backstop existed to prevent exactly this ('never silently skip a changed file').

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, including blocks=true entries that mean 'cannot conclude pass'. The loop at L103-105 now ignores them, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hardcoded to `[]` at L113. The critic is never told about these gaps. Its output `pruned.residual_risks` is the only input deriveVerdict sees (L122), so a deep pass that refused to clear its hotspot can still end in PASS. Before this change, the residuals were collected and sent on (`residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`; `residual_risks: residuals`).

findings.title: Keep whyItBreaks in dedup key to avoid merging distinct findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key is now only file, lineStart, category and the first 60 characters of the normalized title. Two different defects reported by separate hotspot passes with the same anchor line, category and title prefix (for example, two P2 'Validate input ...' findings at one line) now collapse into one, and the dropped one never reaches the critic. The old key included the first 80 characters of whyItBreaks, which kept them apart.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution in the per-hotspot deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code ran `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` on deep.md, which shows the template has a {{FOCUS}} placeholder. With that call removed, every large-PR deep pass gets the literal text `{{FOCUS}}` instead of the user's focus or "(none)". The model never sees the requested focus, and it sees an unfilled template token. Small PRs still get `focus` because reviewSmall serializes the whole bundle (lines 52-55). The same `--focus` request therefore works or silently does nothing depending only on whether the patch is over 30000 chars or 10 files (isLarge, lines 30-32).

findings.title: Forward focus/deep to the map pass bundle again
findings.whyItBreaks: mapBundle (lines 83-89) no longer includes `focus` or `deep`, so the map model that picks the hotspots can't see either option. Hotspots are the only files that get a full deep review, apart from the low-risk tail (lines 96-110). In large-PR mode no other code reads `bundle.deep`, so deep=true now has no effect there. The small-PR path still passes both fields (lines 52-55). How much this changes hotspot ranking depends on how map.md uses these fields, which this checkout doesn't include, so the impact is smaller than the deep-prompt finding.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep propagation in the large-PR map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `focus`/`deep` from `mapBundle` (lines 83-89) and removes the `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", ...)` call from the deep prompt chain (lines 117-121). `reviewSmall` (lines 52-55) still serializes the whole `bundle`, `focus` and `deep` included, into review.md. So what the user asked to focus on is honored only when `isLarge(bundle)` is false (patch ≤30000 chars and ≤10 files, lines 25-32). Once a PR crosses that size, the map and deep passes never see `focus`/`deep`. If deep.md still contains the `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder, the model also gets the literal unreplaced token. The user gets no error and no warning; the review just quietly stops being focused, and that depends on PR size.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep propagation in the large-PR map and deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, reviewLarge put `focus` and `deep` into mapBundle and filled `{{FOCUS}}` in deep.md with `bundle.focus ?? "(none)"`. The head deletes all three lines (hunks at old lines 89-90 and 122). For any PR where isLarge is true (patch over 30000 chars or more than 10 changed files, lines 30-31), the user's focus no longer reaches the map prompt (mapBundle, lines 82-89) or the per-hotspot deep prompt (lines 117-121). If deep.md still contains `{{FOCUS}}`, the model now receives that placeholder unfilled. reviewSmall (lines 52-55) still serializes the whole bundle, focus included, so whether the flag works depends on PR size. Nothing errors or warns.

findings.title: Round to total seconds before splitting minutes to avoid "1m 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: The minutes are taken from the raw ms, and only the leftover is rounded. When the leftover is 59500–59999ms it rounds up to 60. So ms=119500 gives minutes=1, seconds=round(59.5)=60, printed as "1m 60s" (the old code printed "2m 0s"). ms=59500 gives "60s" (the old code printed "1m 0s"). This is a regression in the per-call and total durations shown in the markdown review output (render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: Round to whole seconds before splitting minutes to avoid '1m 60s'
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes = floor(ms/60000), then rounds (ms % 60000)/1000. Any remainder of 59500ms or more rounds up to 60 seconds, but the minute count is not carried. Two examples: ms=119500 gives '1m 60s' (the base code gave '2m 0s'), and ms=59500 gives '60s' (the base code gave '1m 0s'). Two places in renderMarkdown show these impossible values: the per-call durations (line 75) and the total duration (line 80).

findings.title: Round to whole seconds before splitting minutes to avoid "Xm 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes come from Math.floor(ms/60000) before rounding, and seconds come from Math.round((ms%60000)/1000) after. If the leftover is 59500ms or more, seconds rounds up to 60 and nothing carries it into minutes. Examples: ms=119500 gives minutes=1, seconds=round(59.5)=60, so it renders "1m 60s" (the old code gave "2m 0s"). ms=59600 renders "60s" (the old code gave "1m 0s"). This shows up in the per-call stats and the total duration line of the rendered review (render.ts:75, :80). Only display is affected; no data or control flow changes.

findings.title: Restore rejection of zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the guard from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets 0 through. The exported name `parsePositiveInteger` and the error text `requires a positive integer` both promise a value greater than 0. Number('') and Number('   ') both evaluate to 0, so an empty or whitespace-only input now returns 0 instead of throwing. External callers relying on the exported contract get a non-positive value. The input error is hidden behind a value that looks legitimate.

findings.title: Restore rejection of zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` at line 32 changes what this exported public function returns. Before, '0', '' and '   ' all threw `${label} requires a positive integer`. Now each one returns 0, because Number('') and Number('   ') are both 0 and 0 passes Number.isInteger. The function name and the error text at line 33 both still promise a value greater than 0, so external callers that rely on that guarantee now get a silent 0 instead of an error.

findings.title: Restore rejection of zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard at line 32 changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so the input "0" now returns 0 instead of throwing. JavaScript's Number() also turns "" and " " into 0, so empty or blank inputs that used to be rejected now return 0 too. The exported function's name and its own error text at line 33 ("requires a positive integer") still promise a strictly positive result. So any caller of this public function now gets back a value that breaks the contract, where before it got an error. The problem is visible within this one file.
